title: Intumescent Cataract: Clinical Mastery & Surgical Management
summary: An intumescent cataract represents a lens in the rapid, advanced stages of maturation, characterized by cortical liquefaction and increased lens volume. Understanding the 'intumescent crisis' is critical to avoiding devastating surgical complications like the 'Argentinian Flag Sign'.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Intumescent cataract occurs when the lens protein undergoes osmotic degradation, creating high-molecular-weight protein aggregates that exert significant oncotic pressure. This draws aqueous humor into the lens, causing cortical swelling (intumescence), anterior capsular stretching, and shallowing of the anterior chamber.

sections.title: Clinical Features
content: Markedly reduced visual acuity (often CF or HM)

rows: Acute angle closure with swollen lens
Nucleus settles inferiorly in liquefied cortex

sections.title: Surgical Hazards: The Argentinian Flag Sign
content: High Intralenticular Pressure: Leads to uncontrolled radial tears of the anterior capsule.
Argentinian Flag Sign: Radial tears extend to the lens equator; the anterior capsule retracts, creating a 'flag' appearance.
Zonular Instability: Resulting from prolonged lens swelling.
Posterior Capsule Rupture: High risk during hydrodissection.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Step 1: Perform preoperative IOP lowering (Mannitol IV, topical anti-glaucoma meds).
Step 2: Create a small initial capsulorhexis (or use high-viscosity OVD).
Step 3: Puncture the capsule to aspirate liquefied cortex, decompressing the lens.
Step 4: Once decompressed, extend the capsulorhexis to the desired diameter.
Step 5: Utilize 'bimanual' or 'femtosecond laser-assisted' capsulotomy (FLACS) if available.

content.explanation: S: Stabilize IOP, W: Withdraw fluid (cortex), E: Endothelial protection (OVD), L: Laser-assisted or micro-incision preferred, L: Lens removal (phacoemulsification).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the fellow eye: Intumescence is frequently bilateral.
Use heavy-molecular-weight viscoelastic (e.g., Healon5) to maintain anterior chamber depth.
Avoid hydrodissection in the intumescent phase—hydrodelineation is preferred once decompressed.
Consider pars plana vitrectomy for lens aspiration if zonular support is severely compromised.
